Being Yourself

Glasses, a different language at home, an unusual family shape: your child discovers that being different is a way of belonging.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

“Why do you wear glasses?” “Why do you speak a different language at home?” “Why do you have two mums?” — children ask directly, with no unkind intent, but sometimes the question lands right on a sore spot. Maybe it's the hearing aid that stands out, the grandmother raising your child instead of a parent, or simply a passion for spiders that nobody else in the classroom shares. Your child notices, consciously, for the first time: I am different from most others — and does not yet know whether that is good or bad.

Between ages 4 and 9, a child's own identity is beginning to form, and part of that is perceiving themselves in relation to the group. Children this age notice differences very precisely and address them directly, without the social restraint most adults show. This directness is rarely rejection — usually it is pure curiosity — but it can still feel exposing to the child on the receiving end, especially before they know their own response to it.

A story can show that being different is simply part of life, rather than a problem that needs solving. Your child watches a hero who stands out in the same way they do, and sees this character belong precisely because of the difference, not despite it. This identification shifts the perspective: from being different as a flaw to being different as part of what makes someone who they are. With repeated reading, this perspective settles in, ready for the next time an awkward question comes up.

In the personalized story, your child is the hero, with their own face and their own particular difference on every page — whether glasses, language, family shape, or interest. They experience curious questions coming their way, respond to them with quiet confidence, and discover that the very thing that makes them different is a reason to belong. The story frames being different as something that connects rather than separates. The first personalized story is free, so you can discover it together before deciding on more.

Talk about your child's particular difference at home, openly and matter-of-factly, rather than avoiding it — that way your child has a simple, honest answer ready when the question comes up at school. “I wear glasses so I can see well, just like some people don't need them” is usually enough. Encourage your child to allow questions rather than hide — curiosity is usually easy to answer. And watch whether your child withdraws or gets avoided because of the difference; if so, it is worth talking to the teacher.

What your child learns

Self-acceptance, explaining yourself with confidence, welcoming curiosity, sense of belonging.

Recommended age

4-9 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I explain to my child why they are different from other children?

Best done openly and matter-of-factly, with a simple, honest explanation your child can remember, such as “I wear glasses so I can see well.” That way your child has their own answer ready when the question comes up at school.

What if other children tease my child about a particular difference?

Distinguish between curious questions, which are usually harmless, and repeated teasing, which weighs on your child. If teasing persists, it is worth talking to the teacher so the class can address the topic together.

At what age do children notice they are different from others?

Usually between ages 4 and 9, as their own identity forms more strongly and children begin consciously comparing themselves to the group. The more naturally being different is discussed at home, the more calmly your child handles it at school.

Should I encourage my child to allow questions about their difference?

Yes — most questions are pure curiosity, not rejection, and are usually easy to answer. When your child has a short, confident answer ready, the question loses much of its sting.

Can a story help if my child withdraws because of their difference?

It shows your child a character who belongs despite — or precisely because of — their difference, which can shift how they see their own situation. The first personalized story is free; if the withdrawal continues for weeks regardless, also talk to the teacher.
